title: Turn Half-Empty School Wings Into Child Care
one_liner: A turnkey operator that leases empty classrooms in half-empty Title I elementary schools and runs licensed infant, toddler and before/after-school care in them.
customer: School districts that lease the space (landlord side). Revenue comes from parents (including those on state child-care subsidies), state pre-K funds, and employers or the district itself buying slots for staff.
problem: Birth-rate decline has left many elementary schools 20 to 40 percent empty, and districts are closing buildings. Yet the neighborhood has no infant care, teachers quit over child care, and before/after-school waitlists run for months. Empty rooms cost the district no visible money, so nobody champions them, and district counsel treats a sublease as a liability risk.
solution: Sell a feasibility and licensing audit ($5k to $15k) covering egress, restrooms, square footage per child, fencing, a separate entrance, and the fire marshal. Then operate the program as a license-holding subtenant. Staff it with cross-trained paras and neighborhood parents. Accept subsidy vouchers and state pre-K slots. Give priority to school staff and Title I families, and keep before- and after-school care in the same building. The district gets rent plus a utilities share, and the operator keeps a thin margin.
why_now: Enrollment declines and school-closure fights are peaking. The 2025 tax law raised the employer child-care tax credit starting in 2026, which helps districts and employers underwrite staff slots. Several states are expanding subsidized or universal child care. Federal after-school funding uncertainty in 2025 also opened a gap for paid programs.
revenue_model: Tuition and subsidy revenue for the operator. One-time feasibility and licensing fees. Optional management fee if a nonprofit or district holds the license.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone talks about reusing closed schools. The money is in schools that stay open but are half-empty, where a wing can be subleased tomorrow with no rezoning. Elementary buildings already meet many child-care code items: kid-height restrooms, exits, a playground and a kitchen. The principal knows this from living in the building. The blocker is the district's lease template and its fear of liability, and both are solvable with paperwork.
first_30_days: Map licensing rules in one state and find a nonprofit child-care operator willing to hold the license. Pitch 5 superintendents and principals with a two-page space-utilization audit and a sample lease. Sell three $5k feasibility audits to fund the pilot, and use waitlists from existing before/after-school programs as proof of demand.

title: Idle-Still Co-Packing for Zero-Proof Brands
one_liner: Turn distilleries' idle stills and bottling lines into contract capacity for dealcoholized and botanical spirit brands.
customer: Craft and mid-size distilleries with underused capacity, and zero-proof beverage brands that need production.
problem: US spirits sales fell 15.4% and Diageo's US tequila fell 23% as GLP-1 use spreads, leaving distilleries with fixed costs and empty lines.
solution: A capacity broker and operations layer that matches idle distilleries to zero-proof and functional-tonic brands, handles TTB and formulation paperwork, and standardizes QA and scheduling.
why_now: GLP-1 adoption is now visibly cutting alcohol volumes, and the non-alcoholic segment is growing but short of contract capacity with spirit-grade distillation.
revenue_model: 10-15% take on co-pack contracts plus fees for compliance and formulation services.
non_obvious_insight: The first casualties of GLP-1 in beverages are asset-heavy distillers, whose stills are worth more as co-packers to the segment that is replacing them. Grain and agave growers downstream are the next to feel it.
first_30_days: Interview 20 distilleries about idle capacity, line up 5 zero-proof brands with pending production needs, and run one paid pilot batch with a partner distillery.

title: Loss-Draft as a Service for Servicers
one_liner: After a hail or wildfire claim, insurer money is trapped in slow servicer loss-draft processes. Digitize milestone releases so contractors get paid in days, not months.
customer: Mortgage servicers' loss-draft departments, and roofing and repair contractors who work insurance claims.
problem: Insurance claim checks are co-payable to the mortgage lender. Servicers hold the funds and release them in draws after inspections, taking weeks to months. Contractors demand money upfront, homeowners run out of patience, and disputes spread (State Farm hail-claim lawsuits are widening from Oklahoma).
solution: Digital loss-draft. The homeowner uploads the claim payment, funds sit in a servicer-controlled escrow, and milestone releases are verified via geo-tagged photo and video review. Contractors are paid instantly via RTP or FedNow, and the servicer gets a compliance dashboard on cycle times.
why_now: Claim disputes are surging and State Farm is adding 3,000 claims staff (Insurance Journal, 2026-09-25). Instant rails are mature, and servicers face regulatory scrutiny on loss-mitigation timelines (verify the specific rules).
revenue_model: $150-$400 per claim from the servicer, or 0.5-1.0% of proceeds, plus a 1% instant-pay fee to contractors.
non_obvious_insight: Servicers hold large claim balances but run loss-draft as a paper-heavy cost center. Contractors accept lower prices for fast, certain payment, which also lowers repair cost and dispute rates.
first_30_days: Approach five mid-size servicers' loss-draft heads with a free diagnostic on average days to disbursement. Sign a pilot for one catastrophe event. Recruit roofing contractor associations in hail-prone states to onboard.

title: Cremation Memorial Rooms in Vacant Office Space
angle: Pairing 2: Real estate x death/estates/wealth transfer
one_liner: Pay-per-event celebration-of-life rooms in empty ground-floor and office space for families choosing cremation, with an optional urn-niche wall run through a licensed cemetery partner as the long-term annuity.
customer: Families arranging cremation memorials, and direct-cremation providers and independent funeral homes without a venue. Landlords, lenders and special servicers with vacant space earn a revenue share. A licensed cemetery or church partner operates the niches.
problem: Cremation is about 63% of dispositions and heading to 82% by 2045, so the traditional chapel is redundant, but families still need somewhere to gather and somewhere to keep the ashes. 58% of consumers have attended a service at an unconventional venue, and families pay $2-5K for hotel ballrooms and restaurants. Office vacancy is 17.8% nationally, office CMBS delinquency is 13.2% with $39B maturing within 12 months, and urban cemeteries are out of land.
solution: Lease or license vacant space on short terms and fit it out as a 40-80 seat memorial room with AV for tribute video, catering and celebrant partners. Sell event packages wholesale to direct-cremation and funeral-home partners and directly to families ($1,500-3,500). In phase 2, add a niche wall sold as perpetual-care niches through a licensed cemetery operator, since a niche needs a fraction of the land of a burial plot. Zoning and state cemetery law vary, so licensing runs through the partner.
why_now: Cremation crossed 60% and consumer interest in alternatives is rising. Special servicers of distressed office loans will take short-term income from otherwise dead space. Direct-cremation providers are crowded and need a differentiator beyond price. SCI is growing on pricing while volumes fall, which leaves the low-cost end unserved.
revenue_model: Event fees, wholesale packages for funeral homes and direct-cremation providers, a 10-20% commission or operating share on niche sales, and landlord revenue-share deals. Later, employer celebration-of-life benefits.
non_obvious_insight: Cremation removed the need for the funeral home's most expensive asset, the chapel and its land, but not the human need to gather and to keep remains, which now needs roughly one fiftieth of the space. That makes converted office and retail space, not a cemetery, the right home.
first_30_days: Get a 90-day pop-up license for a vacant ground floor in a mid-size downtown. Sign two celebrants and a caterer. Offer wholesale rates to five direct-cremation providers and run three events at cost. Meet a licensed cemetery operator to scope the niche-wall pilot and the state licensing path.

title: Fair Witness: Insured Human Eyes for Remote Deals
one_liner: Heinlein's Fair Witnesses (professionals who report only what they observe) as a bonded, API-callable network that confirms the physical facts of remote transactions for people and buying agents.
customer: High-value peer-to-peer and consignment resellers (watches, pro camera gear, instruments, equipment), small landlords and property managers (move-in and move-out deposit disputes), insurers, and procurement teams or agents that need physical-world confirmation of goods received or site status.
problem: Remote deals stall on the physical world. Photos are easy to fake with generative editing, and signed-capture standards are not enough on their own (a researcher demonstrated forgery of C2PA credentials on Android in August 2026). Existing inspection services are siloed by category.
solution: Train and certify witnesses (retired inspectors, notaries) in a strict 'observe, do not infer' protocol. Capture happens on attested devices with a server-issued freshness challenge (a random code shown in frame, live geo and time nonce), 360-degree and macro video and calibrated measurements. Deliver a structured Witness Report (JSON plus signed media plus witness declaration) via API. Witnesses carry professional liability, and each report is insured up to a stated limit.
why_now: Generative editing has made photo evidence untrustworthy, while hardware-signed capture (Pixel 10 with C2PA) is only partly reliable. Agentic purchasing means software is becoming the buyer that needs a physical-world oracle, and no one supplies one with liability behind it.
revenue_model: $45-150 per visit, a monthly platform fee for API and marketplace integrations, and an insurance margin on the report guarantee.
non_obvious_insight: Camera signatures alone cannot carry trust. Trust is procedure plus a named person plus a liability plus freshness, which is exactly Heinlein's fair witness. Because witnesses give facts, not opinions, they are cheap to train (a few hours) and legally credible as fact witnesses. To avoid being another freelancer marketplace, staff is certified and insured, protocol-bound and sold through an API.
first_30_days: Recruit and certify 30 witnesses in one metro. Partner with two consignment resellers or a small-landlord association. Run 200 paid visits at about $60 and publish an anonymized accuracy and dispute-rate report.

title: Sundowning Night Companion Speaking in Family's Voice
one_liner: A bedside device that detects night waking and reorients a person with dementia in a voice they consented to, escalating to a caregiver or remote night aide.
customer: Family caregivers of people with moderate dementia at home (about 15% provide 60+ hours a week), memory-care communities with thin night ratios, and home-care agencies with overnight cases.
problem: Night waking is a top reason families place a loved one. Overnight aides cost $300-450 a night, and families otherwise absorb 3 am crises. Generic AI companions are seen as deceptive or are not built for dementia.
solution: A bedside speaker or tablet with radar or audio wake detection plays short, clinically scripted reorientation lines in a familiar voice (for example a spouse or child), seeded by a 'voice will' the person records and approves while they still have capacity. It escalates to the caregiver's phone with two-way voice, then to a paid remote night aide, and logs sleep patterns for the neurologist. Guardrails: no impersonation of the deceased, and clinician sign-off.
why_now: Voice cloning from seconds of audio and on-device speech models are cheap in 2026. NY, FL and NJ are giving away ElliQ, showing public payers buy companionship tech, and 23% of 65+ now use ChatGPT, so acceptance is rising.
revenue_model: $199 hardware plus $39-59 a month for families, $30-50 per bed per month for memory care, and remote night-aide add-on fees.
non_obvious_insight: Ethics is the product: an advance 'voice will' turns a controversial deception into a consented comfort, like an advance directive for how you want to be soothed. Night is the least automated and most expensive shift.
first_30_days: Build on a commodity smart speaker with scripted lines, recruit 10 families through Alzheimer's support groups and one neurologist, and measure night-waking events over four weeks. Convene a geriatric psychiatrist and an ethicist as advisors.

title: Remote-Driven Tractors for the Door-to-Door Leg
one_liner: Teleoperated tractors, driven from desks by remote drivers, that shuttle trailers between autonomous-truck terminals and customers' docks within about 30 miles.
customer: Autonomous-truck operators that need a handoff solution, carriers with hub networks, shippers with private yards, and ports and rail ramps.
problem: Hub-to-hub autonomy leaves door-to-door legs with 'hundreds of dollars' of human transfer cost per handoff, yet most freight is door-to-door. Short-haul and drayage driver turnover is high.
solution: Start on private yards, where no on-road rules apply, with retrofit teleop kits, multi-carrier connectivity and automatic safe-stop on link loss. A remote driver handles moves back to back with no deadhead, and automation covers straight segments. Extend later to short, permitted public-road hops at low speed. Price per move below a local yard driver plus deadhead.
why_now: Aurora (about 200 driverless trucks, 30,000 planned), Einride and Gatik are scaling the hub model, and the handoff economics are unresolved. Remote driving has been operating commercially in Europe and Las Vegas, and multi-carrier bonding makes latency manageable. Public-road legality for teleoperated heavy trucks in the US is unclear and needs checking.
revenue_model: $/move pricing, a monthly retainer per terminal, and equipment lease on the retrofit kits.
non_obvious_insight: The industry frames the last leg as an automation problem, but it is a utilization problem. One remote driver can serve several times more moves than a local driver who deadheads between yards, so teleop can beat both a human and a full autonomy stack on price for the next several years.
first_30_days: Sign a private yard (a rail ramp or DC with 20+ yard moves a day), retrofit one tractor with a rented teleop kit, and run a week of shadow operations. Price the pilot at about 20% below the current yard-jockey cost.

title: Verified Pay Receipts for Truck Driver Hiring
one_liner: Drivers upload settlement stubs and AI turns them into the true, receipts-backed pay per mile and per hour away from home for every carrier, sold as a hiring credential and as income proof for lenders.
customer: Honest mid-size carriers (50 to 1,000 trucks) that pay $6k to $15k to hire each driver and can't prove their pay claims are real. Secondary buyers are mortgage and auto lenders (bank-statement and non-QM brokers) who serve drivers.
problem: Recruiter ads say 'up to 75 cents a mile, $100k+' but realized pay is often 20 to 35% lower after unpaid or practical-versus-paid miles, unpaid detention, chargebacks and deductions. Driver turnover at big truckload carriers runs near 90%, and job ads are so discredited that honest carriers can't stand out. Drivers whose pay is structured as tax-free 'per diem' also see a low W-2 and get denied mortgages after 20 years of work. Estimates say the English-proficiency and non-domiciled CDL crackdowns will pull 214,000 to 437,000 drivers (5 to 12% of CDL holders) from the supply over 2 to 3 years, so carriers are competing harder for domestic drivers.
solution: A mobile app where drivers photograph settlement stubs and pay statements. AI extracts paid miles, deadhead, detention, deductions, per diem and time away from home, and computes effective take-home per hour on the road, not just per mile. Public carrier pages show verified figures such as '312 verified drivers, median $0.61 per paid mile, $17.40 per hour away'. Carriers that look good pay for a 'Verified Pay' badge and applicant funnel. A second product builds an income-verification packet from stubs and deposit statements for lenders. Fraud controls include stub-format checks, duplicate detection and consistency with driver-reported miles.
why_now: Shrinking driver supply from the 2025 to 2026 English-proficiency out-of-service enforcement (proposed codification rule published Aug 10, 2026) and the Feb 2026 non-domiciled CDL restrictions means cost-per-hire is rising. Vision-model OCR of messy pay stubs is now cheap and accurate. Truth-in-leasing rules already require itemized settlements, so the raw material exists.
revenue_model: Carrier subscriptions of $500 to $3,000 a month for the verified page, analytics and applicant funnel. Lender referral fees of $300 to $1,000 per funded mortgage or truck loan. Free for drivers, which keeps the data supply growing.
non_obvious_insight: Drivers don't compare carriers by ads, they ask in the truck-stop lot 'what do you actually clear?' The only artifact they trust is a pay stub. The honest carriers are the ones locked out of trust, so they are the natural paying customer. The true unit of pay is dollars per hour away from home, because 14-hour clocks, detention and unpaid waiting eat the mileage math. And per-diem income structures are a hidden mortgage trap that a stub-based income packet can fix.
first_30_days: Post in trucker Facebook groups, Reddit and TikTok: 'Upload your stub, see your real rate vs. what your carrier advertised.' Aim for 500 stubs in 30 days. Publish a 'State of Real Pay' report ranking 20 named carriers and pitch it to trade press (Overdrive, CDLLife, FreightWaves). Sell 'Verified Pay' badges to the 5 mid-size fleets whose numbers look best, and sign one bank-statement mortgage broker for lender leads.

title: Digital Journeyman: Ride-Along Capture for Apprentices
one_liner: Retiring tradespeople wear chest cameras for a few job days, and AI turns the footage into a code-aware 'digital master' that also verifies apprentices' on-the-job hours and technique.
customer: Electrical, plumbing and HVAC contractors and apprenticeship sponsors (JATCs, IEC and ABC chapters), community-college trade programs; retiring journeymen are paid royalty recipients.
problem: Trade apprenticeships take 4-5 years and are bottlenecked by scarce journeyman mentors, many retiring, while the sponsor bottleneck is supervision. OJT hours are logged by hand and cannot be verified, and mentoring quality is inconsistent. The entry path for electricians has about 72.7k openings a year.
solution: V1: apprentice phone or chest-cam capture that produces AI-verified OJT hour logs by task type for sponsor reporting. V2: an 'ask the master' agent trained on captured ride-alongs plus the locally adopted code edition, with escalation to a live mentor. V3: form-check feedback on tasks like conduit bending and terminations. Retiring journeymen earn per-use royalties.
why_now: Video-understanding models can now parse hours of messy jobsite footage, camera-equipped smart glasses reached consumers in late 2025, and data-center demand is stretching journeymen thin. Apprenticeship policy support is growing.
revenue_model: $30-60 per apprentice per month paid by sponsors or contractors, capture-project fees for retiring-mentor programs, and licensing of the annotated video library to trade schools.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce input in the trades is not information but supervised repetition. Verified hours and over-the-shoulder feedback multiply each journeyman's supervisory capacity, and retiring masters' tacit knowledge is a wasting asset worth capturing in the next two years.
first_30_days: Partner with one IEC or ABC chapter or contractor. Equip 10 apprentices with $60 chest-mount phone rigs. Pay 3 retiring journeymen to record about 40 job-hours. Deliver an OJT hour-log report a sponsor accepts and charge $40 per apprentice per month. Handle site-owner consent up front.

title: Warranty Clock Recovery Audits for Idle Halls
one_liner: A contingency-fee service that finds and files the warranty claims on energized-but-empty data halls before OEM warranty clocks silently expire.
customer: Colocation developers, powered-shell landlords, neocloud operators and enterprise owners with phased or delayed-tenant builds, especially those with halls commissioned 6-14 months ago and not yet loaded. The owner pays a percentage of recovered value, plus an optional per-asset tracking subscription.
problem: Warranty clocks on generators, UPS systems, chillers, CRAH/CDUs, switchgear, and batteries usually start at shipment or startup, not when a tenant loads the hall. With delayed leases and mid-build AI redesigns, halls sit energized and idle for months. Many defects only show under real load (UPS capacitors, chiller compressors, wet-stacking gensets, breaker trip curves, coolant chemistry). By the time the tenant ramps, the warranty has expired. The turnover package is 50,000+ pages of PDFs that ops never reads, the punch-list deferrals are lost, and OEM maintenance records required to keep coverage valid are often missing. Nobody owns the clock.
solution: Ingest POs, OEM warranty terms, startup sheets, Cx reports, shipping documents and maintenance logs with an LLM pipeline to build a serial-number-level warranty ledger with real expiry dates and voiding conditions. Flag anything expiring within 120 days. Run a targeted load-dependent-defect inspection before expiry (thermography, oil and coolant samples, capacitor and battery checks, breaker testing). File claims, negotiate warranty start-date deferrals or extensions with the OEM while leverage still exists, and fix missing maintenance-record gaps. For new builds, sell a PO-stage clause pack that defers warranty start to beneficial occupancy.
why_now: There is a glut of speculative shells and delayed tenant handoffs. Reporting in 2026 shows close to half of planned US builds slipping, with only about a third of 2026 target capacity under active construction. That means many halls are powered, commissioned and idle. Equipment was bought at peak prices with tariffs on steel, aluminum and copper, so each lapsed warranty is worth more. LLMs can now read messy closeout binders cheaply, which was the labor bottleneck for audits like this.
revenue_model: 25-30% of recovered value or avoided cost on claims and negotiated extensions, no fee if nothing is recovered. Optional $150-400 per asset per year tracking subscription. $15K-40K fixed-fee closeout audits for owners who want certainty. PO-stage clause-pack consulting for developers.
non_obvious_insight: The warranty is the only major asset on a data center balance sheet that expires silently. OEMs will defer warranty start dates at PO time, but almost no one negotiates it because the project team is fighting for delivery slots, not paperwork. After the fact, the owner's ops team inherits the docs with no idea when the clocks started. The money is in the punch-list items that were 'to be fixed later' and the load-dependent defects that only appear after the hall is finally used.
first_30_days: Find 3 owner-operators through PM and Cx network contacts with halls energized 8-11 months ago and not fully loaded. Offer a free 10-day scan of their closeout binders in exchange for a contingency agreement on any claims. Build the extraction pipeline on real binders (gensets, UPS, chillers first). Deliver a 'expiring within 90 days' hit list and file the first claims before the first invoice.

title: Physically Verified Protocol Skills for Lab Agents
angle: Pairing 1: AI agents & agent economy x Biotech tools / synbio / lab automation
one_liner: A registry of agent-executable bench protocols where every version has actually been run on real instruments in independent labs, with signed control readouts, like CI badges backed by experiments.
customer: AI-native biotech startups, academic labs and core facilities running agent-directed workflows on liquid handlers (Opentrons OT-2/Flex, Hamilton, Tecan), plus cloud-lab operators. Buyers are lab managers and automation leads. Individual protocol authors are the supply side.
problem: Agent 'skills' registries are the new package supply chain (about 20% of the OpenClaw skill registry was reportedly malicious, and Okta paid about $200M for Permiso to sandbox skills). In biology a bad skill is not just a leaked token. It is a wasted week of bench time, a contaminated line, or a biosafety event. The last roughly 10% of manual steps in a 5,000-action workflow is tacit knowledge nobody writes down. Anthropic found that robotic automation fit ad hoc molecular-biology workflows poorly, and that expert review and bench work were the bottleneck rather than compute.
solution: Publish protocols as versioned skills: robot script, agent-readable instructions, parameter bounds, expected control values and hazard flags. A release counts as 'verified' only after it runs on at least 3 independent partner instruments and posts raw plate-reader or qPCR files with pass/fail on Z' and control CVs. Agents (or their human owners) can only pull skills above a reproducibility threshold. Static checks flag off-protocol reagent additions, unusual volumes or temperatures and dual-use red flags. Start with about 25 workhorse assays: Golden Gate/Gibson assembly, transformation, qPCR setup, viability, ELISA and Bradford.
why_now: The skills-as-supply-chain scare of 2026 and the Permiso acquisition prove buyers will pay to trust agent skills. Frontier labs and startups are now wiring agents to physical labs (Anthropic's wet lab, Medra, Lila, Transfyr's $25M seed to capture bench actions). Nobody sells verified physical execution, only software scanning.
revenue_model: Subscription per lab ($300-1,000/month for verified-skill access and update alerts); per-protocol certification fees paid by protocol authors and vendors ($1-3K per validation cycle); revenue share to partner validation labs; enterprise private registry for pharma automation groups.
non_obvious_insight: In software, tests are free, so registries compete on code. In biology the test is an experiment, so the moat is a network of physical validation sites and the accumulated failure data, not the code. Whoever owns the 'passes on real hardware' stamp owns trust in agentic bench work, and it also becomes the natural biosafety screen for skills.
first_30_days: Recruit 3 academic labs that already own OT-2s (they are common and often underused). Pick 10 protocols and run each 3 times per site. Publish the raw data and pass rates publicly as the marketing. Offer free verified skills to 30 labs via bioRxiv/Reddit/Slack communities, then charge $500/month for early access to new verified skills, alerts and private forks. Target 10 paying labs by month 3.

title: Group-Block Attrition and Force Majeure Claims Desk
one_liner: A 48-hour, outcome-priced desk that tells meeting and wedding planners whether the 2026 shocks let them escape or shrink hotel attrition penalties, and files the notices on time.
customer: Association and corporate meeting planners without in-house counsel (100-1,000 attendees), destination-wedding planners, DMCs, and youth-sports or choir tour operators holding hotel room blocks.
problem: Hormuz closure (2 Mar 2026), jet-fuel-driven capacity cuts and fare hikes, and UAE hospitality disruption mean groups cannot fill contracted blocks, while booking lead times shrank from 37.5 to 33 days. Attrition clauses often penalize around 20% shortfalls, and force-majeure wording and notice deadlines, not the law, decide outcomes. Small planners miss the 7-30 day notice windows and pay in full.
solution: Upload the contract for a clause map covering the attrition table, cure and mitigation duties, force-majeure triggers, and deadlines. The desk generates the notice letters, sends deadline alerts, and provides a negotiation script and a walk-away vs renegotiate calculator. A partner hospitality lawyer handles escalations at a fixed fee. Cases where the hotel resold freed rooms at higher rates argue mitigation, not force majeure.
why_now: The 2026 disruption produced a wave of disputes between now and winter events. Europe summer ADR rose 4-6% and Turkey flights rose 25% as trips rerouted. In those markets hotels can resell freed blocks at higher prices, which weakens their damages claims.
revenue_model: $390 flat for the clause map and deadline pack, about 15% of penalties avoided as a success fee, and fixed-fee lawyer escalations. An annual $1,200 deadline-tracker subscription is aimed at DMCs.
non_obvious_insight: The strongest argument is often mitigation, not force majeure. In rerouting hot spots the hotel resells rooms at higher rates and cannot claim losses it did not suffer. The moat is a dataset of clause wording and outcomes, plus never missing a deadline.
first_30_days: Recruit 20 planners from association-executive and wedding-planner forums with a free 'contract triage' of one block. Have one hospitality lawyer review the template letters. Convert the first 5 to paid flat-fee packs and log every outcome to build the clause database.

title: Common Rooms: Community-Share Buyouts of Neighborhood Bars
one_liner: A studio that helps retiring owners sell beloved bars, cafes, bookstores and cinemas to hundreds of neighbors through community-share offers, then supplies a manager and shared back office.
customer: Owners over 60 of profitable independent third-place businesses who can't find a buyer, plus neighbors who buy $100-500 shares. Commercial landlords are a third stakeholder.
problem: Boomers own most main-street businesses and many will simply close, because a qualified buyer with SBA-loan credit is rare. Communities lose their remaining third places while loneliness is a public-health issue.
solution: The UK community-pub playbook, using US tools: a Reg CF offering (up to $5M a year), an LLC or co-op with member voting, a pre-launch pledge drive to prove 300-800 neighbor investors, a professional general manager, and a shared back office (bookkeeping, permits, POS, purchasing) across all venues in the portfolio. Community shares replace acquisition debt so the business isn't forced to service a loan.
why_now: Peak-65 owners are exiting in volume, Reg CF and its platforms are mature, and retail vacancy plus loneliness make the case politically easy. In the UK, community pubs have raised about GBP 35M from 37,500+ shareholders, but the US has no equivalent operator.
revenue_model: Success fee of 3-5% of the raise, a monthly management-services contract ($1.5-3k) per venue, and vendor rebates from pooled purchasing.
non_obvious_insight: Community ownership doesn't sell returns, it sells guaranteed regulars. 500 shareholders who each show up twice a month are a customer base that exists before the doors reopen, and that is why these businesses survive at much higher rates than buyer-owned ones. The moat is the repeatable legal and marketing kit and the shared back office, not any single deal.
first_30_days: Choose one metro and phone 25 owners over 60. Find three with positive cash flow willing to sell at roughly 2-3x seller's discretionary earnings. Launch a pledge page ('would you put $250 into saving X?') to prove demand, and retain securities counsel for a templated Reg CF filing. Charge a small engagement fee up front, with the balance due on close.

title: Pre-Loss Home Reconstruction Dossiers for Insurance Claims
one_liner: Rebuild, in the exact quality and condition language insurers can't wave away, what a destroyed home actually had, using old appraisals, listing photos, permits and imagery.
customer: Public adjusters and policyholder-side insurance attorneys handling total-loss wildfire, hurricane and tornado claims pay $900-2,500 per dossier. Direct-to-homeowner is $495 for a basic version. Independent insurance agents later buy a 'pre-loss baseline' for their high-value clients.
problem: After a total loss, the insurer's estimate assumes builder-grade finishes and smaller square footage. The survivor's photos and receipts burned, so 'like kind and quality' becomes a memory-versus-spreadsheet fight worth tens or hundreds of thousands of dollars per house. Public adjusters reconstruct from Zillow photos and homeowner recollection, which adjusters on the other side discount.
solution: A retrospective, signed 'as-was' dossier delivered in about 5 business days. Sources: (1) any prior purchase or refinance appraisal the homeowner has (borrowers are entitled to copies) or can get through the lender or servicer; (2) archived MLS photos and remarks from the last sale; (3) permit and remodel history; (4) assessor quality and size records; (5) historical aerial and street-level imagery. A licensed appraiser assigns the standard Q1-Q6 quality and C1-C6 condition ratings, lists the finishes and features, and estimates replacement cost at that quality level.
why_now: The January 2025 Los Angeles fires destroyed roughly 16,000 structures, and many claims are still being contested in late 2026. Every wildfire and hurricane season adds more total losses. Insurers are tightening costs and leaning on adjuster software. Photo and record archives from prior sales are now digital and searchable, so the reconstruction is a 5-day job.
revenue_model: Flat fee per dossier only. USPAP forbids contingent appraisal fees, and independence is the product's credibility. Volume pricing for public adjuster firms. $99/yr 'baseline vault' (current LiDAR, photos and Q/C ratings) sold through independent insurance agents in wildfire and hurricane zones, who carry E&O exposure when clients are underinsured.
non_obvious_insight: The best pre-loss evidence in America already exists, sitting in lender closing files, appraisal workfiles kept five years and old MLS pages. Nobody connects it to claims. A neutral licensed appraiser's dated interior photos and Q/C ratings carry far more weight with an insurer than a homeowner's testimony. Those disputes are won at the finish level (cabinetry, flooring, millwork), not on square footage, and the appraiser's rating vocabulary is what claims examiners recognize.
first_30_days: Recruit 3 appraisers in Los Angeles County who lost work. Build one dossier template. Offer 5 free pilot dossiers to 2-3 public adjuster firms and one policyholder attorney working Altadena or Pacific Palisades cases, and measure how much the insurer's revised offer moves. Then charge $1,500 per dossier and use the measured lift as the sales pitch.

title: Reuse Exchange for Closing Parish Contents
one_liner: A cataloging, canon-law compliance and matching service that moves stained glass, statues, vestments, bells and furniture from closing parishes to churches that need them.
customer: Dioceses and archdiocesan closure committees, religious orders and denominational property offices, with receiving parishes, new chapels and immigrant or missionary congregations on the other side.
problem: Closure committees catalog contents by hand, and surplus goes out through liturgical dealers. Sacred items risk profane use (confessionals turned into restaurant phone booths, upsetting donors' families), canon law restricts profane sale, and organs and murals often cannot be saved.
solution: A photo-cataloging app with AI-assisted identification, provenance and donor-plaque tracking, blessed-status and canon-law flags, and a bishop approval workflow. A gated marketplace of vetted receiving churches, including overseas missions served by consolidated containers. Optionally digitally sample condemned organs before removal.
why_now: Parish consolidations continue while church attendance is flat (Pew: 33% attend monthly). Dioceses are cash-strapped and want revenue from contents. Photo AI and container consolidation are now cheap.
revenue_model: A per-closure project fee ($5-25k), 10-15% commission on sales, and a freight-consolidation margin on overseas shipments.
non_obvious_insight: Buyers are not the scarce input. Trust and compliance are: sellers need proof items will not be profaned, and buyers in growing regions need provenance and affordable freight. A vetted receiving-church network is the asset incumbents (liturgical dealers) lack.
first_30_days: Offer 3 diocesan property offices a free catalog of one closing church. Build a list of 50 missionary and immigrant-parish buyers through religious-order mission offices. Ship the first container.

title: Provenance Stamps for AI-Drafted Official Products
one_liner: A document layer that makes AI-assisted analytic and official products visibly claim-by-claim traceable, and refuses to export as official until unsupported claims are resolved.
customer: State and regional fusion centers, police intelligence units, commercial OSINT and threat-intel shops selling to government, and city attorneys' offices. DoD follows later via integrators.
problem: A SOCOM analyst's chatbot invented a ship's cargo manifest, and it was formatted into an official-looking intelligence summary before aircraft were airborne. Insiders say better models will fix hallucination. The real failure is laundered credibility: AI-formatted output looks signed and trusted.
solution: A Word and Docs add-in that tags every sentence as source-linked, analyst-asserted or model-generated. Model-generated claims carry a visible marker. Official templates and PDF export are blocked until each claim has a source or a named human sign-off. It produces a hashed provenance record for later review.
why_now: GenAI.mil hit more than 2M users in one week, and 100k custom agents exist. The SOCOM story is public, and government AI-governance guidance is hardening. Buyers can now cite a concrete incident.
revenue_model: $40-90 per user per month, with agency site licenses of $50-250K. Enterprise add-ons for audit reporting.
non_obvious_insight: The fix is friction, not accuracy. Sell a product that deliberately makes AI-drafted content look unofficial until a human has vouched for it, so trust cannot be laundered through formatting.
first_30_days: Ship the add-in for one document type, such as a threat bulletin. Recruit 3 fusion centers and 2 OSINT vendors as design partners. Build a demo that replays the SOCOM failure and shows it being blocked.

title: Tariff Surcharge Clawback for B2B Buyers
one_liner: A contingency-fee service that mines a buyer's 2025-26 supplier invoices for 'tariff surcharge' lines and recovers a share of the IEEPA refunds those suppliers are now collecting.
customer: Multi-unit restaurant and retail franchisees, contractor purchasing co-ops, and mid-market distributors' customers that paid itemized tariff, freight or 'inflation' surcharges to suppliers who were the importer of record. They pay a 20-30% success fee on money recovered.
problem: IEEPA duty refunds go only to the importer of record (IOR) or a party the IOR designates. Buyers who paid the tariff as a surcharge or a higher price get nothing unless they ask. AutoZone booked about $96M and Cracker Barrel $15M, with MillerKnoll $16.5M and Worthington $4M. Downstream buyers have no visibility into what their suppliers recovered and no process to ask for it.
solution: Read-only inbox and AP connectors pull 2025-26 invoices and extract surcharge, 'tariff', 'duty' and 'trade cost recovery' line items. The system estimates each supplier's IEEPA exposure from public import-manifest data. It checks the supplier's terms for pass-back language, such as 'surcharge will be removed or refunded if tariffs are rescinded'. It then generates a claim letter with an offer to accept credit memos or to have the supplier name the buyer as the CBP Form 4811 notify party so the refund routes to the buyer. A second module audits new diesel and fuel surcharges against the contract formula and the EIA diesel index. Claims are sent to the top 20 suppliers per buyer, and unclaimed money is tracked to closure.
why_now: CBP's CAPE portal opened in 2026 and is issuing refunds within 60-90 days of an accepted declaration. Refunds are landing in Q3-Q4 2026 P&Ls as one-time gains. Suppliers are least defensible in the first months after booking a windfall and will negotiate to keep customer goodwill. Diesel is $6.53/gal, up $2.78 year over year, so a wave of fresh surcharge invoices is arriving that nobody audits.
revenue_model: A 20-30% contingency fee on recovered refunds and credits, plus $199-$999/month for continuous surcharge auditing (fuel, energy, 'regulatory recovery' fees) once the first recovery lands.
non_obvious_insight: The refund windfall is a transfer from customers to importers, and the CFOs say so. AutoZone's CFO said 'the refund environment was deflationary, and the industry likely would have raised prices faster if both retailers and suppliers hadn't received cost relief' (https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/09/22/autozone-azo-q4-2026-earnings-call-transcript/). Cracker Barrel booked a $15M refund and MillerKnoll $16.5M, worth 180 bps of gross margin (https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/09/23/cracker-barrel-cbrl-q4-2026-earnings-call-transcript/ and https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/09/22/mlkn-q1-2027-earnings-call-transcript/). CBP states 'Only the IOR ... or the authorized customs broker ... may file' and never mentions downstream buyers, couriers or DDP shipments (https://www.cbp.gov/trade/programs-administration/trade-remedies/ieepa-duty-refunds). Every downstream claim is therefore a negotiation, and the buyer who holds the 2025 invoices has the leverage. Nobody is selling that to the buyer side. The legal caveat is that the buyer needs an explicit surcharge line or contract language to have a real claim, so the product should target only those cases.
first_30_days: Recruit 5-8 restaurant franchisee groups or contractor purchasing co-ops through franchisee associations and buying-group managers, with a free 'we only get paid if you get paid' offer. Export 2025 AP data or forward invoice PDFs, then have an analyst plus an LLM extraction script build a surcharge ledger for the top 15 suppliers each. Send the first 30 claim letters with a one-page template that cites the refund program and asks for credit or 4811 routing. Have a supply-chain lawyer review the template. Aim to close the first paid recovery within 60-75 days.

title: Funeral Committee Escrow and Fixed-Price Vendor Network
one_liner: A per-funeral M-Pesa vault where contributions can only be released to pre-priced vendors with two-of-three committee approvals, ending the 'where did the burial money go' fights.
customer: The family and burial committee (treasurer, chair, village elder, workplace welfare group) organising a rural funeral, usually with a Nairobi or diaspora fundraising arm. Vendors (tent and chair hire, caterers, coffin makers, embalmers, hearse and PA operators) are the second paying side.
problem: A rural funeral is often a family's biggest single cash event, drawing hundreds of mourners and costing multiples of a year's farm income. It is run on WhatsApp groups and an exercise book. Treasurer fraud and 'the money vanished' accusations are common and can split families for years. Vendors quote inflated prices to grieving families who cannot shop around, mortuary storage fees accrue daily so decisions are rushed, and families often sell land, borrow against coop shares or take mobile loans to close the gap. Existing crowdfunding tools collect money but do nothing about how it is spent.
solution: Each funeral gets a dynamic M-Pesa paybill account and a WhatsApp bot (English, Swahili, Sheng). The committee picks from fixed-price packages (basic, standard, large) with vendor prices published. Every payout to a vendor till needs two of three designated approvers by USSD PIN, and a live ledger is visible to all contributors. The bot also handles pledge tracking, reminders in the Nairobi and home committees, the mortuary and transport schedule, and a post-funeral accounting statement. Money sits in a licensed payment provider's trust account, not on the startup's balance sheet.
why_now: M-Pesa paybill, till and B2B payout APIs are mature enough to make programmable escrow cheap, and the WhatsApp Business API is inexpensive. LLMs now let a bot handle Swahili and Sheng committee chatter. The post-2023 cost-of-living squeeze makes families more sensitive to funeral overspending and to selling land to pay for it. Funeral crowdfunding has trained diaspora and urban Kenyans to give online, but nobody controls the spend side.
revenue_model: About 2-3% fee on money flowing through the vault plus negotiated vendor margins or referral commissions of roughly 8-12% on vendor spend. Later upsells are funeral cover (partnered with a licensed insurer), memorial pages, and body-transport routing between Nairobi and up-country.
non_obvious_insight: Money that is locked to named vendors is welcome, not resented: it protects the treasurer from the 'sharing tax' of relatives and neighbours asking for cash, and from accusations. In effect the product sells social protection, not payments. Funerals are also where families mortgage their long-term farm assets, so reducing funeral overspend is a farm-resilience product that VCs would never classify as agtech.
first_30_days: Recruit 8-10 vendors (tents, catering, coffins, hearse) along one corridor such as Nairobi to Murang'a or Nyeri and agree fixed package prices. Onboard the first 5 funerals by offering free setup through church welfare groups, alumni groups and your own contacts, using a manual approval flow on top of an existing paybill provider. Charge the fee only after a funeral closes with a clean statement, and use those statements as proof for the next 50.

title: Inverter-Telemetry Credit Bureau for African Solar
angle: Pairing 2: Energy transition & grid x Emerging markets leapfrogging
one_liner: Turn the cloud data that hybrid inverters and batteries already stream into a consented energy cash-flow score, so lenders, insurers and installers can finance an asset boom that official statistics cannot see.
customer: Solar and battery asset financiers, MFIs and banks in Nigeria, Kenya, Ghana and South Africa, plus installers who need financing to close sales. Insurers and DFIs paying for verified performance come later.
problem: Africa installs 17 GW of solar in 2026 (+45%), 75% of the growth is distributed, and it imports more battery dollars than panels. Ember says its estimates are 2x official figures and only 14 of 54 countries reported 2025 data, so credit bureaus and insurers have nothing to price on. Installers cannot get customers financed, and lenders cannot see collateral health or borrower activity.
solution: With owner consent gathered through the installer, pull production, load, battery health, uptime and location data from inverter and BMS clouds (Victron VRM, Solarman for Deye, Growatt, Huawei, Solis). Compute diesel displacement and savings, a load-profile proxy for business activity (cold-room cycles, salon hours), collateral health and tamper flags, and installer quality scores. Sell an API and dashboard to lenders, with remote-lock hooks and insurer feeds as add-ons.
why_now: Distributed solar plus batteries has become private infrastructure. Stationary packs fell 45% to about $70/kWh, African equity funding is concentrated while debt replaces equity (so lenders need collateral visibility), and India's UPI fee change shows how fragile transaction-data underwriting is. The US also needs neutral telemetry, since Sunrun and Tesla's 16.8 GW capacity-as-a-service has no disclosed verification standard.
revenue_model: $2-6 per scored asset per month or per-report fees, a 1-2% origination fee on financing it unlocks, installer SaaS, insurer data licensing, and later verification fees from results-based financing programs.
non_obvious_insight: The best alternative-credit dataset in Africa is already being emitted by hardware nobody thinks of as a bureau. Energy consumption is a real-time proxy for small-business activity, and the inverter is both the collateral and the sensor. Because the data layer is vendor-neutral, it can later certify firm distributed capacity for utilities and hyperscalers, something Tesla and Enphase cannot credibly do for each other's fleets.
first_30_days: Integrate two APIs (Victron VRM and Solarman/Deye) and sign 3 installers in Lagos, Nairobi or Johannesburg with 300+ systems between them. Collect customer consents through the installers' apps and publish a free installed-base map. Take the top-scoring 30 customers to one MFI or asset financier for a pilot loan pool, charging a 2% origination fee.

title: Auracast Hearing Access for Churches and Senior Centers
one_liner: Turnkey Bluetooth Auracast broadcast installs that let people with hearing loss hear services, meetings and group activities directly in their own hearing aids and earbuds.
customer: Houses of worship, senior centers, libraries, community halls and municipal meeting rooms, paying $1.5-6k for install plus $50-150 a month managed service.
problem: Hearing loss is a leading modifiable dementia risk and a quiet driver of withdrawal: people stop going to services, dinners and meetings because they cannot follow. Fewer than one in three adults who could benefit use hearing aids. Legacy hearing loops are costly and often fail unnoticed, and FM systems require borrowing clunky receivers. Venues with amplified sound face ADA assistive-listening obligations that many ignore.
solution: Pre-configured Auracast transmitters (line-in or audio-over-IP) installed in a day, with QR signage ('join the broadcast'), usher training, room-level coverage checks and a remote-monitoring dashboard so it keeps working. Multi-channel support allows a second-language stream (English and Spanish) from the same room.
why_now: Auracast (LE Audio broadcast) is shipping in current hearing aids, phones and earbuds. OTC hearing aids (2022) and AirPods Pro hearing-aid features (Sep-Oct 2024) expanded the user base. Loneliness is now a WHO-measured metric, and venues want visible ways to include older attendees.
revenue_model: Install fee plus recurring managed-service subscription. Referral fees from audiologists and hearing-aid manufacturers seeking demand generation.
non_obvious_insight: The hidden loneliness intervention is upstream of any program: tens of millions of people with hearing loss quietly stop attending. Fixing the room is cheaper than fixing the person, and Auracast collapses the cost of doing it.
first_30_days: Buy three transmitters (about $300-600 each). Install free in three churches or senior centers in one metro with an audiologist partner, capture attendance and testimonials, then sell ten installs at about $2.5k through denominational newsletters and audiologist referrals.
